claims.claim: The bHLH domain is responsible for dimerizing with other bHLH proteins and for binding to Ephrussi box DNA elements to regulate transcription.
claims.source: PTHS-causing mutations typically impair the function of the bHLH domain, which is responsible for dimerizing with other bHLH proteins and for binding to Ephrussi box DNA elements to regulate transcription (Dennis et al., 2019; Sepp et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Dennis et al., 2019; Sepp et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Hundreds to thousands of genes lie downstream of TCF4.
claims.source: However, hundreds to thousands of genes lie downstream of TCF4 (Doostparast Torshizi et al., 2019; Forrest et al., 2013; Hill et al., 2017; Xia et al., 2018), making it nearly impossible to find transcriptional modifiers to correct their expression levels.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Doostparast Torshizi et al., 2019; Forrest et al., 2013; Hill et al., 2017; Xia et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Normalizing expression of the disease-causing gene in postnatal life could provide therapeutic benefits in animal models of Rett and Angelman syndromes.
claims.source: For example, studies in animal models of other single-gene neurodevelopmental disorders, including Rett and Angelman syndromes, have shown that normalizing expression of the disease-causing gene in postnatal life could provide therapeutic benefits (Guy et al., 2007; Silva-Santos et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Guy et al., 2007; Silva-Santos et al., 2015).

claims.claim: There is no evidence for disease-related neurodegeneration in PTHS individuals or mouse models.
claims.source: While synaptic defects have been observed in mouse models of PTHS, there is no evidence for disease-related neurodegeneration in PTHS individuals or mouse models (Rannals et al., 2016; Thaxton et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Rannals et al., 2016; Thaxton et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Synaptic defects have been observed in mouse models of PTHS.
claims.source: While synaptic defects have been observed in mouse models of PTHS, there is no evidence for disease-related neurodegeneration in PTHS individuals or mouse models (Rannals et al., 2016; Thaxton et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Rannals et al., 2016; Thaxton et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Subtle upregulation of Tcf4 expression by knocking down Hdac2 partially rescued learning and memory in adult PTHS model mice.
claims.source: In support of this idea, subtle upregulation of Tcf4 expression by knocking down Hdac2 has been shown to partially rescue learning and memory in adult PTHS model mice (Kennedy et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Kennedy et al., 2016).

claims.claim: TCF4/Tcf4 expression in the human/mouse brain peaks perinatally, before subsequently declining to basal levels that are sustained throughout adulthood.
claims.source: This question is particularly intriguing given observations that TCF4/Tcf4 expression in the human/mouse brain peaks perinatally, before subsequently declining to basal levels that are sustained throughout adulthood (Phan et al., 2020; Rannals et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Phan et al., 2020; Rannals et al., 2016).

claims.claim: The levels of full-length Tcf4/TCF4 were reduced by approximately half in Tcf4STOP/+ mouse brain compared to Tcf4+/+ mouse brain.
claims.source: As predicted from our design, the levels of full-length Tcf4/TCF4 were reduced by approximately half in Tcf4STOP/+ mouse brain compared to Tcf4+/+ (wildtype control) mouse brain and fully normalized by crossing Tcf4STOP/+ to Actb-Cre+/- mice (Figure 1B, Tcf4+/+: 1.0 ± 0.09, n = 7; Tcf4STOP/+: 0.61 ± 0.07, n = 7; Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre: 1.04 ± 0.09, n = 5, and Figure 1C, Tcf4+/+: 1.0 ± 0.07, n = 7; Tcf4STOP/+: 0.58 ± 0.05, n = 7; Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre: 1.07 ± 0.07, n = 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR and Western blot shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claims.claim: Crossing Tcf4STOP/+ to Actb-Cre+/- mice fully normalized Tcf4/TCF4 levels.
claims.source: As predicted from our design, the levels of full-length Tcf4/TCF4 were reduced by approximately half in Tcf4STOP/+ mouse brain compared to Tcf4+/+ (wildtype control) mouse brain and fully normalized by crossing Tcf4STOP/+ to Actb-Cre+/- mice (Figure 1B, Tcf4+/+: 1.0 ± 0.09, n = 7; Tcf4STOP/+: 0.61 ± 0.07, n = 7; Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre: 1.04 ± 0.09, n = 5, and Figure 1C, Tcf4+/+: 1.0 ± 0.07, n = 7; Tcf4STOP/+: 0.58 ± 0.05, n = 7; Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre: 1.07 ± 0.07, n = 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR and Western blot shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claims.claim: GFP signal was detected throughout the Tcf4STOP/+ mouse brain.
claims.source: GFP signal, a proxy for presence of the STOP cassette, was detected throughout the Tcf4STOP/+ mouse brain.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: GFP signal was absent from Tcf4+/+ and Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre brain sections.
claims.source: By contrast, this signal was absent from Tcf4+/+ and Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre brain sections, indicating efficient excision of the GFP-STOP cassette and concomitant reinstatement of biallelic Tcf4 expression in the Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre model mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Male and female Tcf4STOP/+ mice had reduced body and brain weights.
claims.source: Male and female Tcf4STOP/+ mice had reduced body and brain weights, whereas Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre mice had similar body and brain weights to their littermate controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C.

claims.claim: Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre mice had similar body and brain weights to their littermate controls.
claims.source: Male and female Tcf4STOP/+ mice had reduced body and brain weights, whereas Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre mice had similar body and brain weights to their littermate controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C.

claims.claim: Reduced brain weight in Tcf4STOP/+ mice represents a phenotype with high face validity for human microcephaly.
claims.source: Reduced brain weight in Tcf4STOP/+ mice represents a phenotype with high face validity for human microcephaly (Dupuis et al., 2015; Pulvers et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Dupuis et al., 2015; Pulvers et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Tcf4STOP/+ mice exhibited impaired object location memory.
claims.source: Tcf4STOP/+ interactions with objects located in the familiar and novel positions were of similar duration, suggesting the inability to remember the previously-presented location of the object and suggestive of long-term memory deficits (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from object location memory test shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre mice exhibited normal object location memory.
claims.source: Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre and control mice both interacted to a significantly greater extent with the object located in the novel position, suggesting recovery of normal long-term memory function subsequent to embryonic, pan-cellular Tcf4 reinstatement (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from object location memory test shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Tcf4STOP/+ mice showed increased activity and total distance travelled compared to Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre mice in the open field test.
claims.source: We then assessed locomotor and exploration activity by the open field test and found that Tcf4STOP/+ mice showed increased activity and total distance travelled compared to Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre mice, which exhibited control levels of activity (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field test shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Tcf4STOP/+ mice exhibited poor performance in the nest building task over the 4-day testing period.
claims.source: Tcf4STOP/+ mice exhibited poor performance in the nest building task over the 4-day testing period, using roughly half the nest material used by control mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nest building test shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The nest building phenotype was completely rescued in the Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre model.
claims.source: This phenotype was completely rescued in the Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre model (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nest building test shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Tcf4STOP/+ mice spent similar amounts of time in the closed and open arms of the elevated plus maze, indicating an apparent low-anxiety phenotype.
claims.source: We observed Tcf4STOP/+ mice to spend similar amounts of time in the closed and open arms, indicating an apparent low-anxiety phenotype.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from elevated plus maze test shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The low-anxiety phenotype appeared to be normalized in Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre mice.
claims.source: This behavioral feature also appeared to be normalized in Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre mice, spending proportionally more time in the closed arms (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from elevated plus maze test shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Tcf4STOP/+ mice exhibit physiological and behavioral phenotypes like those observed in other mouse models of PTHS.
claims.source: Collectively, our results confirm that Tcf4STOP/+ mice exhibit physiological and behavioral phenotypes like those observed in other mouse models of PTHS (Kennedy et al., 2016; Thaxton et al., 2018), demonstrating the efficacy of the transcriptional STOP cassette in blocking TCF4 function.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to prior literature (Kennedy et al., 2016; Thaxton et al., 2018) and experimental data from this study.

claims.claim: TCF4 is present in excitatory and inhibitory neurons of the forebrain.
claims.source: A previous anatomical study shows that TCF4 is present in excitatory and inhibitory neurons of the forebrain (Kim et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Kim et al., 2020).

claims.claim: Tcf4 transcript levels are higher in excitatory and inhibitory neurons than most other cell types in the neonatal and adult mouse brain.
claims.source: Moreover, single-cell transcriptomic studies in the neonatal and adult mouse brain indicate that Tcf4 transcript levels are higher in excitatory and inhibitory neurons than most other cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Loo et al., 2019; Zeisel et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of single-cell transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior literature (Loo et al., 2019; Zeisel et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Tcf4STOP/+::Neurod6-Cre mice exhibited significantly higher activity levels than control mice in the open-field test.
claims.source: In the open-field test, we found that Tcf4STOP/+::Neurod6-Cre mice exhibited significantly higher activity levels than control mice (Tcf4+/+ and Tcf4+/+::Neurod6-Cre, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and similar activity levels as Tcf4STOP/+ mice, indicating that embryonic reinstatement of Tcf4 in forebrain glutamatergic neurons failed to rescue the hyperactivity phenotype (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field test shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Embryonic reinstatement of Tcf4 in forebrain glutamatergic neurons failed to rescue the hyperactivity phenotype.
claims.source: In the open-field test, we found that Tcf4STOP/+::Neurod6-Cre mice exhibited significantly higher activity levels than control mice (Tcf4+/+ and Tcf4+/+::Neurod6-Cre, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and similar activity levels as Tcf4STOP/+ mice, indicating that embryonic reinstatement of Tcf4 in forebrain glutamatergic neurons failed to rescue the hyperactivity phenotype (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field test shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Embryonic Tcf4 reinstatement in GABAergic neurons is insufficient to fully prevent the hyperactivity phenotype.
claims.source: Activity levels in Tcf4STOP/+::Gad2-Cre mice were statistically indistinguishable from either control mice (Tcf4+/+ and Tcf4+/+::Gad2-Cre, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) or Tcf4STOP/+ mice (Figure 2B), suggesting that embryonic Tcf4 reinstatement in GABAergic neurons is also insufficient to fully prevent the hyperactivity phenotype.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field test shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Tcf4 reinstatement in glutamatergic neurons improved object location memory.
claims.source: Tcf4 reinstatement in glutamatergic neurons improved object location memory, whereas Tcf4 reinstatement in GABAergic neurons failed to fully prevent location memory impairments (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from object location memory test shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Tcf4 reinstatement in GABAergic neurons failed to fully prevent location memory impairments.
claims.source: Tcf4 reinstatement in glutamatergic neurons improved object location memory, whereas Tcf4 reinstatement in GABAergic neurons failed to fully prevent location memory impairments (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from object location memory test shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Reinstating Tcf4 in glutamatergic neurons restored the low-anxiety phenotype.
claims.source: In the elevated plus maze task, we found that Tcf4STOP/+::Neurod6-Cre and control mice exhibited increased closed arm activity compared to Tcf4STOP/+ mice, showing that reinstating Tcf4 in glutamatergic neurons restored the low-anxiety phenotype (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from elevated plus maze test shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Tcf4STOP/+::Gad2-Cre mice exhibited reduced closed arm activity compared to controls, indicating persistence of the reduced anxiety-like phenotype despite reinstatement of Tcf4 in GABAergic neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, Tcf4STOP/+::Gad2-Cre and Tcf4STOP/+ mice exhibited reduced closed arm activity compared to controls (Figure 2D), indicating persistence of the reduced anxiety-like phenotype despite reinstatement of Tcf4 in GABAergic neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from elevated plus maze test shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Embryonic reinstatement in glutamatergic neurons was sufficient to prevent the impaired nest building phenotype in PTHS model mice.
claims.source: Finally, we observed that Tcf4STOP/+::Neurod6-Cre mice used a similar amount of nest materials as their respective controls, while Tcf4STOP/+::Gad2-Cre mice used more nest materials than Tcf4STOP/+ mice, but significantly less material than controls (Figure 2E), demonstrating that embryonic reinstatement in glutamatergic neurons was sufficient to prevent the impaired nest building phenotype in PTHS model mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nest building test shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Tcf4 is expressed at all stages of oligodendrocyte development.
claims.source: In addition to being expressed in neurons, Tcf4 is expressed at all stages of oligodendrocyte development (Kim et al., 2020; Phan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Kim et al., 2020; Phan et al., 2020).

claims.claim: The loss of TCF4 has been associated with decreased oligodendrocytes and impaired myelination.
claims.source: Consistent with this expression pattern, the loss of TCF4 has been associated with decreased oligodendrocytes and impaired myelination (Phan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Phan et al., 2020).

claims.claim: Reinstating Tcf4 in Olig2-expressing cells did not improve behavioral performance on open field and object location memory task in PTHS model mice.
claims.source: We found that reinstating Tcf4 in Olig2-expressing cells did not improve behavioral performance on open field and object location memory task in PTHS model mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Normalizing Tcf4 expression from both glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons might be required to fully rescue behavioral phenotypes.
claims.source: In sum, our findings suggest that normalizing Tcf4 expression from both glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons, and perhaps other cell types, might be required to fully rescue behavioral phenotypes.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing partial rescue with cell-type-specific reinstatement.

claims.claim: Cre expression was not significantly detected from relatively medial sagittal sections of P4 and P7 mouse brain following ICV injection of PHP.eB-hSyn-Cre on P1.
claims.source: We failed to detect significant Cre signals from relatively medial sagittal sections of P4 and P7 mouse brain, despite being able to observe a local distribution of Cre-expressing cells in the brain regions near the lateral ventricle injection site (Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3B-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C.

claims.claim: Cre mRNA and protein distribution across the forebrain remained sparse until at least P10.
claims.source: Cre mRNA and protein distribution across the forebrain remained sparse until at least P10 (Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3B-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Cre was visibly and more broadly expressed in the hippocampus and throughout the cortical layers by P17.
claims.source: But, Cre was visibly and more broadly expressed in the hippocampus and throughout the cortical layers by P17 (Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3B-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The biodistribution of Cre protein at P60 was widespread in the brain, with particularly prominent expression in the forebrain compared to subcortical regions.
claims.source: The biodistribution of Cre protein at P60 was widespread in the brain, with particularly prominent expression in the forebrain compared to subcortical regions (Figure 3D–F), which is similar to patterns of endogenous TCF4 distribution (compare Figure 3D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3D-F.

claims.claim: RT-qPCR results confirmed increased relative expression of Tcf4 transcripts from P10 and P17 Tcf4STOP/+ brains treated with PHP.eB/Cre.
claims.source: The RT-qPCR results confirmed increased relative expression of Tcf4 transcripts from P10 and P17 Tcf4STOP/+ brains treated with PHP.eB/Cre (Figure 3G, Tcf4STOP/+ + Vehicle at P10: 1.0 ± 0.09, n = 3; Tcf4STOP/+ + PHP.eB/Cre at P10: 1.05 ± 0.05, n = 3; Tcf4STOP/+ + Vehicle at P19: 1.0 ± 0.04, n = 4; Tcf4STOP/+ + PHP.eB/Cre at P19: 1.39 ± 0.15, n = 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: PHP.eB/Cre treatment fully rescued activity levels in Tcf4STOP/+ mice.
claims.source: Similar to vehicle- or virally treated Tcf4+/+ mice, Tcf4STOP/+ mice treated with PHP.eB/Cre exhibited normal activity levels in the open field test, whereas vehicle-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice were hyperactive (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field test shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: PHP.eB/Cre treatment fully rescued long-term memory performance in Tcf4STOP/+ mice.
claims.source: In addition to normalizing activity levels, PHP.eB/Cre treatment also fully rescued long-term memory performance in Tcf4STOP/+ mice compared to vehicle-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from object location memory test shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: PHP.eB/Cre-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice spent relatively more time in the closed arms than the open arms in the elevated plus maze.
claims.source: In the elevated plus maze, PHP.eB/Cre-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice spent relatively more time in the closed arms than the open arms, similar to vehicle- and PHP.eB/Cre-treated Tcf4+/+ mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from elevated plus maze test shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: PHP.eB/Cre treatment supported progressive improvement of nest building behavior in Tcf4STOP/+ mice.
claims.source: Lastly, we found that PHP.eB/Cre treatment supported progressive improvement of nest building behavior in Tcf4STOP/+ mice. Specifically, although both Tcf4STOP/+ groups appeared to be similarly lacking in the execution of this behavior at baseline, but over the course of 1 week, PHP.eB/Cre-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice proved capable of incorporating nest materials to a similar degree as vehicle- or virally treated Tcf4+/+ mice (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nest building test shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: PHP.eB/Cre-mediated postnatal reinstatement of Tcf4 did not correct small body and brain sizes.
claims.source: While PHP.eB/Cre-mediated postnatal reinstatement of Tcf4 partially or fully recovered performance on a variety of behavioral phenotypes in PTHS model mice, we found that small body and brain sizes were not corrected (Figure 4F–G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F-G.

claims.claim: Treating Tcf4STOP/+ mice with PHP.eB/GFP did not rescue abnormal behavioral phenotypes.
claims.source: Treating Tcf4STOP/+ group with PHP.eB/GFP did not rescue abnormal behavioral phenotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that behavioral rescue in PTHS model mice was driven by Cre-mediated excision of the STOP cassette in the Tcf4 allele.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Long-term memory deficit and abnormal innate behavior, but not the hyperactive phenotype, were rescued in Tcf4STOP/+::Camk2a-Cre mice.
claims.source: We found that long-term memory deficit and abnormal innate behavior, but not the hyperactive phenotype, were rescued in Tcf4STOP/+::Camk2a-Cre mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Several clinical observations have reported electroencephalographic (EEG) abnormalities, such as altered slow waves, in individuals with PTHS.
claims.source: Several clinical observations have reported electroencephalographic (EEG) abnormalities, such as altered slow waves, in individuals with PTHS (Amiel et al., 2007; Peippo et al., 2006; Takano et al., 2010), yet these phenotypes have not been examined in PTHS model mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Amiel et al., 2007; Peippo et al., 2006; Takano et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Significant decreases in Tcf4STOP/+ LFP power were evident in the theta (5–8 Hz) band.
claims.source: Significant decreases in Tcf4STOP/+ LFP power were evident in the theta (5–8 Hz) band (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LFP recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, E.

claims.claim: Total LFP power was significantly reduced in vehicle-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice compared to vehicle- and virally-treated Tcf4+/+ mice.
claims.source: Upon analyzing LFP recordings in vehicle- and virus-treated groups (Figure 5B–C), we found total LFP power to be significantly reduced in vehicle-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice compared to vehicle- and virally-treated Tcf4+/+ mice, but partially normalized in PHP.eB/Cre-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LFP recordings shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Total LFP power was partially normalized in PHP.eB/Cre-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice.
claims.source: Upon analyzing LFP recordings in vehicle- and virus-treated groups (Figure 5B–C), we found total LFP power to be significantly reduced in vehicle-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice compared to vehicle- and virally-treated Tcf4+/+ mice, but partially normalized in PHP.eB/Cre-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LFP recordings shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The normalization of total LFP power appeared to be largely driven by the normalization of theta band activity.
claims.source: This effect appeared to be largely driven by the normalization of theta band activity (Figure 5E), which was evident across one-minute recording epochs (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LFP recordings shown in Figure 5E-F.

claims.claim: Cre mRNA was still robustly detected in 6-month-old mice, subsequent to viral delivery of the Cre transgene at P1.
claims.source: ISH revealed that Cre mRNA was still robustly detected in 6-month-old mice, subsequent to viral delivery of the Cre transgene at P1 (Figure 6A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 6A-D.

claims.claim: Cre was observed in most cells throughout the layers in the cortex and olfactory bulb.
claims.source: In the cortex and olfactory bulb, Cre was observed in most cells, but certainly not all, throughout the layers (Figure 6C–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 6C-D.

claims.claim: Most pyramidal cells expressed Cre in the hippocampus, but non-expressing cells were evident, especially in the dentate gyrus.
claims.source: Similarly, although we found most pyramidal cells to express Cre in the hippocampus, non-expressing cells were evident, especially in the dentate gyrus (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Reinstating Tcf4 in a subset of neurons can provide therapeutic benefit.
claims.source: This observation suggests that reinstating Tcf4 in a subset of neurons can provide therapeutic benefit.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that not all neurons expressed Cre, yet behavioral rescue was observed.

claims.claim: Tcf4 mRNA expression was approximately 1.3-fold higher in virally treated versus vehicle-treated Tcf4STOP/+ forebrains at P150-P200.
claims.source: We next analyzed Tcf4 mRNA expression from the forebrains of the PHP.eB/Cre-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice. On average, Tcf4 mRNA expression was approximately 1.3-fold higher in virally treated versus vehicle-treated Tcf4STOP/+ forebrains at P150-P200 (Figure 6F, Tcf4+/+ + Vehicle: 1.0 ± 0.18, n = 15; Tcf4STOP/+ + Vehicle: 0.56 ± 0.09, n = 14; Tcf4STOP/+ + PHP.eB/Cre: 0.72 ± 0.12, n = 15).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Grin2a, Mal, Glra3, and Lpar1 were noticeably downregulated in vehicle-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice, but at least partially normalized by PHP.eB/Cre treatment.
claims.source: Each was noticeably downregulated in vehicle-treated Tcf4STOP/+ mice, but at least partially normalized by PHP.eB/Cre treatment (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Normalizing Tcf4 expression in a subset of neurons might be sufficient to rescue behavioral phenotypes in Tcf4STOP/+ mice.
claims.source: These observations suggest that normalizing Tcf4 expression in a subset of neurons might be sufficient to rescue behavioral phenotypes in Tcf4STOP/+ mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the postmortem analyses showing partial normalization of Tcf4 and TCF4-regulated genes.

claims.claim: Genetic reinstatement of Tcf4 in a subset of neurons during early postnatal development corrected multiple behavioral phenotypes in PTHS model mice, including hyperactivity, reduced anxiety-like behavior, memory deficit, and abnormal innate behavior.
claims.source: In this proof-of-concept study, genetic reinstatement of Tcf4 in a subset of neurons during early postnatal development corrected multiple behavioral phenotypes in PTHS model mice, including hyperactivity, reduced anxiety-like behavior, memory deficit, and abnormal innate behavior.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Early postnatal Tcf4 reinstatement corrected altered local field potential activity.
claims.source: Furthermore, early postnatal Tcf4 reinstatement corrected altered local field potential activity and, at the molecular level, TCF4-regulated gene expression changes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LFP recordings shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Early postnatal Tcf4 reinstatement corrected TCF4-regulated gene expression changes at the molecular level.
claims.source: Furthermore, early postnatal Tcf4 reinstatement corrected altered local field potential activity and, at the molecular level, TCF4-regulated gene expression changes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Postnatal genetic therapies to compensate for loss-of-function of TCF4 can offer an effective treatment for PTHS.
claims.source: Our results suggest that postnatal genetic therapies to compensate for loss-of-function of TCF4 can offer an effective treatment for PTHS.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing behavioral and electrophysiological rescue.

claims.claim: Moderately widespread Tcf4 normalization throughout the brain was likely accomplished by P10-P17.
claims.source: We likely accomplished moderately widespread Tcf4 normalization throughout the brain by P10-P17 (Figure 3), which is roughly equivalent to the first 2 years of human life (Wang et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3 and citation to prior literature (Wang et al., 2020).

claims.claim: P10-P17 in mice is roughly equivalent to the first 2 years of human life.
claims.source: We likely accomplished moderately widespread Tcf4 normalization throughout the brain by P10-P17 (Figure 3), which is roughly equivalent to the first 2 years of human life (Wang et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Wang et al., 2020).

claims.claim: Individuals with PTHS have global developmental delay, often presenting itself in the first year of life.
claims.source: Individuals with PTHS have global developmental delay, often presenting itself in the first year of life (Zollino et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Zollino et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Genetic normalization approaches could provide a viable early life treatment opportunity for PTHS.
claims.source: Thus, our study indicates that genetic normalization approaches could provide a viable early life treatment opportunity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing rescue with early postnatal intervention.

claims.claim: Tcf4 expression levels are particularly high in the forebrain.

claims.claim: Reactivating Tcf4 expression in excitatory pyramidal neurons, dentate gyrus mossy cells, and granule cells within the dorsal telencephalon improved memory, anxiety phenotype, and innate behavior.
claims.source: Reactivating Tcf4 expression in excitatory pyramidal neurons, dentate gyrus mossy cells, and granule cells within the dorsal telencephalon, starting from ~E11.5, improved memory, anxiety phenotype, and innate behavior, while reactivating Tcf4 expression in almost all GABAergic neurons throughout the brain at ~E13.5 partially rescued memory and innate behavior (Goebbels et al., 2006; Taniguchi et al., 2011; Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citations to prior literature (Goebbels et al., 2006; Taniguchi et al., 2011).

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citations to prior literature (Goebbels et al., 2006; Taniguchi et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Memory, anxiety-like behavior, and innate behavior might mainly depend on having normal TCF4 levels in excitatory neurons.
claims.source: Given that memory, anxiety-like behavior, and innate behavior were fully rescued when Tcf4 was re-activated only from excitatory neurons, it is reasonable to argue that these phenotypes might mainly depend on having normal TCF4 levels in excitatory neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing full rescue with excitatory neuron-specific reinstatement.

results.result: PTHS is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by TCF4 haploinsufficiency, characterized by developmental delay, intellectual disability, lack of speech, motor incoordination, and other features, with no current effective treatments.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C7-C9 establish the clinical and genetic background of PTHS based on well-cited prior literature. These are established facts about the disease that provide context for the study.

results.result: TCF4 is a bHLH transcription factor whose mutations impair DNA binding and dimerization functions, regulating hundreds to thousands of downstream genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 describe the molecular function of TCF4 based on established literature. These provide necessary background on the genetic mechanism underlying PTHS.

results.result: Prior work suggests that postnatal genetic normalization could be therapeutic for PTHS, as synaptic defects exist without neurodegeneration, and TCF4 expression peaks perinatally then declines.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 establish the rationale for the study based on prior work in related disorders and PTHS models. These citations provide the scientific justification for testing postnatal intervention.

results.result: The Tcf4STOP/+ mouse model exhibits approximately 50% reduction in Tcf4/TCF4 levels, which is fully normalized by crossing to Actb-Cre mice, as confirmed by molecular and immunohistochemical analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22 validate the conditional mouse model with RT-qPCR, Western blot, and GFP immunostaining data (Figure 1B-C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). The data demonstrate appropriate haploinsufficiency and Cre-mediated rescue.

results.result: Tcf4STOP/+ mice exhibit reduced body and brain weights that are normalized in Tcf4STOP/+::Actb-Cre mice, representing a phenotype with face validity for human microcephaly.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by quantitative data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C showing significant differences in body and brain weights. The comparison to human microcephaly is appropriately cited.

results.result: Embryonic pan-cellular Tcf4 reinstatement fully rescues behavioral phenotypes in PTHS model mice, including memory deficits, hyperactivity, impaired nest building, and low-anxiety behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C33 are supported by comprehensive behavioral data in Figure 1D-G showing rescue of object location memory, open field activity, nest building, and elevated plus maze performance. Statistical significance is demonstrated for all phenotypes.

results.result: TCF4/Tcf4 is highly expressed in excitatory and inhibitory neurons of the forebrain, particularly during embryonic and postnatal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 and C83 are supported by prior literature citations and single-cell transcriptomic analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The data justify targeting these neuronal populations.

results.result: Embryonic Tcf4 reinstatement in either glutamatergic or GABAergic neurons alone fails to rescue hyperactivity, suggesting both neuronal types require normal Tcf4 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 and C86 are supported by open field data in Figure 2B showing that neither Neurod6-Cre nor Gad2-Cre reinstatement rescues hyperactivity. The interpretation that both cell types are required is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Embryonic Tcf4 reinstatement in glutamatergic neurons fully rescues memory, anxiety-like behavior, and nest building, while GABAergic reinstatement provides only partial rescue, suggesting these phenotypes depend primarily on excitatory neuron TCF4 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 and C84-C85, C87 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 2C-E showing differential rescue patterns. Glutamatergic reinstatement fully rescues multiple phenotypes while GABAergic reinstatement is less effective. The interpretation is consistent with the data.

results.result: Tcf4 reinstatement in oligodendrocytes does not improve behavioral phenotypes, suggesting that normalizing Tcf4 in both glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons may be required for full rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C showing no rescue with Olig2-Cre. The conclusion that both neuronal types are needed is a reasonable inference from the cell-type-specific experiments.

results.result: Neonatal ICV injection of PHP.eB-hSyn-Cre produces sparse Cre expression until P10, broader expression by P17, and widespread forebrain expression by P60, with corresponding increases in Tcf4 transcript levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 are supported by in situ hybridization, immunofluorescence, and RT-qPCR data in Figure 3B-G showing the temporal progression of Cre expression and Tcf4 reinstatement. The data establish the timeline of viral-mediated gene delivery.

results.result: Postnatal neuronal Tcf4 reinstatement via PHP.eB/Cre fully rescues hyperactivity, long-term memory, anxiety-like behavior, and progressively improves nest building in PTHS model mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 and C72 are supported by comprehensive behavioral data in Figure 4B-E showing rescue of multiple phenotypes. The data demonstrate that postnatal intervention can reverse established behavioral deficits.

results.result: Postnatal Tcf4 reinstatement does not correct reduced body and brain sizes in PTHS model mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C57 is supported by data in Figure 4F-G showing persistent reductions in body and brain weight despite behavioral rescue. This suggests anatomical deficits require earlier intervention.

results.result: PHP.eB/GFP control treatment does not rescue behavioral phenotypes, confirming that rescue is driven by Cre-mediated Tcf4 reinstatement.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is supported by control data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing no rescue with GFP virus. This is an essential control demonstrating specificity of the genetic intervention.

results.result: Postnatal Tcf4 reinstatement in Camk2a-expressing neurons rescues memory and nest building but not hyperactivity.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing selective rescue with Camk2a-Cre. This reinforces that targeting both excitatory and inhibitory neurons provides better outcomes.

results.result: PTHS model mice exhibit reduced hippocampal LFP power, particularly in the theta band, which is partially normalized by postnatal Tcf4 reinstatement.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 and C73 are supported by LFP recording data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing reduced theta power in Tcf4STOP/+ mice and partial rescue with PHP.eB/Cre treatment. This is the first characterization of electrophysiological phenotypes in PTHS mice.

results.result: Six months after P1 viral delivery, Cre is expressed in most but not all neurons in the cortex, olfactory bulb, and hippocampus, suggesting that partial neuronal reinstatement can provide therapeutic benefit.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 are supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 6A-D showing mosaic Cre expression. The inference that partial reinstatement is sufficient is reasonable given the behavioral rescue observed.

results.result: Postnatal Tcf4 reinstatement produces approximately 1.3-fold increase in Tcf4 expression and partially normalizes expression of TCF4-regulated genes (Grin2a, Mal, Glra3, Lpar1) in adult forebrains.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71, C74, and C98 are supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 6F showing partial normalization of Tcf4 and downstream gene expression. This molecular validation supports the behavioral rescue observed.

results.result: The study demonstrates that postnatal genetic normalization of Tcf4 can provide effective treatment for PTHS, with implications for therapeutic development targeting early life intervention in the forebrain.
results.evaluation: Claims C75, C79, C82, and C106-C108 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by the comprehensive behavioral, electrophysiological, and molecular data. The conclusions are appropriately qualified as proof-of-concept in a mouse model.

results.result: Moderately widespread Tcf4 normalization was achieved by P10-P17, roughly equivalent to the first 2 years of human life, when PTHS symptoms typically present.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 are supported by the temporal expression data in Figure 3 and appropriate citation for developmental timing equivalence. This establishes the translational relevance of the intervention window.

results.result: Tcf4 expression is particularly high in the forebrain, and intrathecal ASO delivery produces similar biodistribution, suggesting this approach could be therapeutically viable.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 are supported by citations to prior literature. This provides rationale for future therapeutic development based on the proof-of-concept results.

results.result: TCF4 loss in neurons contributes to PTHS behavioral phenotypes, and mosaic neuronal reinstatement of TCF4 is sufficient to produce phenotypic rescue, indicating therapeutic strategies should target neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 and C102 synthesize the findings from cell-type-specific and viral experiments. The conclusion that neuronal targeting is sufficient is well-supported by the data in Figures 4-5.

results.result: Greater phenotypic rescue might be achieved with additional Tcf4 reinstatement in oligodendrocytes or peripheral tissues, particularly for phenotypes like constipation.
results.evaluation: Claims C92 and C94 are speculative statements about potential improvements. While reasonable hypotheses, they are not tested in this study and represent future directions rather than established results.

results.result: TCF4 is expressed outside the brain, is dosage-sensitive, produces multiple isoforms, and regulates genes involved in synaptic function and neuronal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C93, C95-C97, C100, and C103-C105 provide important context about TCF4 biology based on well-cited prior literature. These establish considerations for therapeutic development.

results.result: The study normalized Tcf4 only in neurons using hSyn promoter, as CAG promoter caused glial activation and toxicity in preliminary experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C99 and C101 describe study limitations and design choices. The toxicity observation with CAG promoter is mentioned as preliminary data with appropriate citation to prior literature on CAG toxicity.
